text: Easy fix for rambling! Just take off a little reward for every word.
Let’s try it. And now Tiny answers in the blink of an eye.
Wow, so fast! And... wrong. Wrong. Wrong!
We told Tiny to be short. We forgot to tell it to be right.
In this episode: how to pay for short answers, without ever paying for wrong ones.
Shorter thinking. Episode two.
First, why bother? Because every word a model writes costs time, and money.
Just the answer: a few tokens. Short working: about twelve times the cost. Long working with re-checks: about a hundred and twenty times.
So... no thinking at all? Just answers?
No. Brief on easy problems. Longer on hard ones. And never trade a right answer for a short one.
Think of a delivery company that pays a bonus for speed.
A parcel that zooms to the wrong address in an hour? No bonus.
Only parcels that reach the right address get paid extra for being fast.
So speed only counts once you’re right.
That’s the golden rule. Length only matters once the answer is right.
So here are two ways to say: be concise. Both only apply to correct answers. Wrong ones always score zero.
Shape one, a length penalty. A right answer starts near one, and loses a little for every token, down to one half.
And a half still beats zero, so being right always wins.
Exactly. Shape two, a budget.
Anything under the limit gets full marks. Go over, and the reward slides down.
So it doesn’t care about forty words versus sixty. It just hates going way over.
Shape three comes from a paper called DAPO. Picture a road with a wall at the end.
Every reply has a hard cap. Up to a hundred and fifty tokens, the road is smooth. No penalty.
Then comes a rumble strip. The penalty ramps down, minus a half, then more.
At two hundred tokens, the wall: minus one, and the reply is cut off.
And this one doesn’t check if the answer is right?
Right. You add it to a correctness reward. You feel the strip before you hit the wall.
Let’s run these on real code. One question, five answers. Four right, of different lengths, and one short wrong one.
Plain correctness can’t tell the four right answers apart. Same score.
Switch on the length penalty, and they line up: shorter right answers score higher. The wrong one stays at zero.
Now remember, GRPO doesn’t use scores directly. It compares each answer to its group’s average.
Look at the very long answer. Two hundred and fifty-nine tokens, and correct.
Which way does it get pushed?
Pause, and have a guess.
A, surely! It got the answer right, so it gets pushed up.
That’s what most people think. But it’s B. Down, a little.
Here’s the group. The scores average out at about point five seven.
Each answer is pushed by how far it sits above or below that average.
The short right answer gets a big push up. The very long right answer?
Its score, point five, is just below the average. So its push is negative. Minus point two one.
So a correct answer gets made a little less likely? Because it was long?
Yes. That’s the power and the danger of a length reward in one picture. On a hard problem, the long answer might be the only one that solved it.
So how do we protect the hard problems?
One fix: compare lengths within each group. On an easy question, the shortest right answer gets the bonus.
On a hard question where every right answer is long, there’s nothing shorter to compare with, so nobody is penalised.
And start gentle. Many people switch the length reward on only after accuracy has climbed.
In TRL, you just pass two reward functions: correctness, and the overlong rumble strip.
Reward weights say how much each counts. Here, being right counts twice as much.
And replies that get cut off at the cap are left out of the loss, instead of counted as failures.
Quick recap.
Length only counts once the answer is right.
You can use a penalty, a budget, or a rumble strip before the wall.
And keep it gentle, because even a right answer can get pushed down.
But here’s the thing. Everything so far, Tiny learns by trial and error.
Thousands of tries, mostly wrong, nudged by a score.
Wait. What if Tiny just copied the homework of a much bigger model? Every step, written out?
DeepSeek tried exactly that, against trial and error, on the same small models.
